GLM-5.3 was released just 7 days ago and was an extremely significant leap compared to GLM-5.2, wh
content:
If it's true that this is indeed GLM-5.4/5.5, then it would change everything, without exaggeration.

GLM-5.3 was released just 7 days ago and was an extremely significant leap compared to GLM-5.2, which was improved solely through real-time modeling (RL). Same base model. And all this in a very short time.

If it's true that GLM-5.4 has become so much better just a week later thanks to RL, it would demonstrate:

1) how much faster the models are now becoming. Not only is there no end in sight, but: now more than ever, exponential growth.

2) It would force OpenAI and Anthropic to release models. Anthropic, in particular, with its upcoming IPO, now has to prove itself. And it would put pressure on slowing down in favor of security.

3) And at least as importantly: the gap between China and the US is shrinking even further, even faster. It seems to be generally accepted that this is a Chinese model. No one suspects it's a Google model.

Given the same tokenizer, it's most likely GLM, and that would be the craziest thing we've seen in a long time for the reasons mentioned above.

But perhaps it's MiMo. Or, quite far-fetched, Ilya Sutskever's SSI model.

It remains exciting. I've rarely seen the community so impressed and confused at the same time. I'm equally confused and impressed.

@davis7 used Fable to determine which model it most closely resembles. A screenshot of the test is attached. h/t Ben Davis

content:
I’ve been saying this for a decade:

AI + multiomics + lifestyle + microbiome + clinical data → precision medicine.

Moderna’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reaching Phase III in melanoma is a major milestone.

And this is NOT ChatGPT/LLM AI.

The exact architecture Moderna uses is proprietary. It could involve custom-built ML models or ensemble approaches like XGBoost, or perhaps SVM.

The AI/ML is solving a fundamentally different problem:

Out of hundreds or thousands of tumor mutations, which ones should we target to generate the strongest immune response?

🧬 Sequence tumor
🤖 Rank neoantigens
💉 Design personalized mRNA vaccine
🛡️ Train T cells
🎯 Combine with immunotherapy

The bigger vision:

Genomics + proteomics + metabolomics + microbiome + lifestyle + longitudinal clinical data → an AI model of the individual.

My hypothesis is that everyone’s immune system and microbiome are unique, and understanding those differences will be central to the next generation of precision medicine, especially in treating cancer and other complex diseases.

AI won't replace doctors.

It may give doctors something far more powerful:

A much deeper understanding of the individual patient!!

#AI #PrecisionMedicine #Cancer

I asked it to build a real-time weather intelligence dashboard with an interactive 3D globe, a forecasting layer that predicts weather 3 days ahead, and a
content:
Claude Code is now scary good at full-stack!

I asked it to build a real-time weather intelligence dashboard with an interactive 3D globe, a forecasting layer that predicts weather 3 days ahead, and an anomaly detector that flags cities whose weather is behaving abnormally.

It came back with a spinning globe that has a day/night cycle using NASA satellite imagery, city lights on the dark side, weather icons that switch between sun and moon based on local time, and a time travel slider that scrubs through 10 days of data.

And when a city's weather breaks from its own normal, it pulses red (abnormally hot) or blue (abnormally cold) right on the globe, updating live and reflecting the anomaly state at any point you drag the slider to.

Claude Code built the whole thing in a single session, including the backend, database, data pipeline, and frontend.

For the database, I needed something fast for time-series workloads since the app ingests hourly weather readings across many cities and serves time-range queries on every slider interaction.

I used Tiger Cloud by @TigerDatabase, which gives you managed TimescaleDB on the Postgres you already know.

Claude Code connected to it through the Tiger CLI MCP server and set up the entire backend directly:

- Provisioned the database service
- Created hypertables for time-partitioned weather storage
- Set up continuous aggregates for pre-computed rollups
- Built the data ingestion pipeline and the full NextJS + ThreeJS frontend

The time travel slider queries thousands of rows on every position change.

On a regular Postgres table, this would require manual partitioning and index tuning to stay fast as data grows.

TimescaleDB partitions the data by timestamp automatically, so each query only hits the relevant time chunk.

Continuous aggregates serve the trend charts, the forecast layer, and the anomaly baselines from pre-computed rollups instead of rescanning raw data on every request.

The video below shows the final build in action, and I worked with the Tiger Data team to put this together.

Tiger CLI is open-source (Apache 2.0) and works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and VS Code.

→ Install Tiger CLI: curl -fsSL https(:)//cli(.)tigerdata(.)com | sh

→ Run tiger mcp install claude-code

→ Give Claude Code a prompt and let it build

OpenAI spent three years and billions of dollars clawing ChatGPT to the #5 spot. Anthropic, Perplexity, and DeepSeek are buying users one expensive click at a time.

X skipped that entire fight. It already had 4.4 billion visits a month and dropped an AI into the middle of them.

Distribution was always the endgame. The labs are learning it the hard way.

Tech debt is annoying, but at least it has a shape. But at the rate at which we are using AI to generate code, we are piling up what I call "slop debt".

It is what happens when most of a codebase is
content:
Tech debt is annoying, but at least it has a shape. But at the rate at which we are using AI to generate code, we are piling up what I call "slop debt".

It is what happens when most of a codebase is generated by an LLM, reviewed by nobody who actually understands it, and merged because the tests passed.

It looks like code. It compiles. It even works, for now. But it was never designed. It was predicted, one relevant-enough token at a time.

These are just some thoughts and observations from watching this happen. I wrote about why slop debt is different from traditional tech debt, and what happens when it compounds.

Give it a read.

content:
Most teams rush to build AI agents before asking the most important question:

❓ Should you even build one?

Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework has a decision tree that cuts through the noise. Here's what it actually says:

🔷 Step 1 — Business Plan Check
If your task is structured or predictable → skip agents entirely. Use GitHub, Microsoft Fabric, or ML models instead.
If it's static knowledge retrieval → build a RAG app, not an agent.

🔷 Step 2 — SaaS Before Custom
Before writing a single line of custom agent code, ask: does M365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Azure Copilot, or Dynamics 365 already solve this?
If yes → use it. If no → now you can build.

🔷 Step 3 — Architecture Decision
Single agent or multi-agent?
Only go multi-agent if you're crossing security/compliance boundaries, involving multiple teams, or planning for serious scale.

Otherwise? Test a single agent first. If it passes → ship it. If it fails → then escalate to multi-agent.

The framework's core philosophy:
👉 Don't build what already exists.
👉 Don't over-engineer what can stay simple.
👉 Let the use case — not the hype — drive the architecture.

This is the kind of structured thinking that separates mature AI adoption from "we just used agents because everyone else is."

💬 Where does your team usually get stuck in this decision process?

Here's how it works:

1. We ask candida
content:
We're using a new method to hire engineers at @HelloUntangle.

I think this playbook will become the standard for hiring technical talent in the age of agents.

Here's how it works:

1. We ask candidates to submit a screen recording of their whole screen, shipping a new feature on a current app they work on. 

Note: This is usually 45 minutes of video - no editing or speeding up - we want to see them thinking, prompting and problem solving with the agent - we also want to see their devops skills.

2. We watch these videos and pick a subset to go through Round 2.

3. Round 2 is giving them a seat on @DevinAI so they have secure access to our repo.

4. We ask them to ship a new real-world feature and get the PR merge-ready.

5. We pay them a fixed fee to do this, and they have 16 hours to complete the work.

6. We watch the videos, review at all the Devin threads, have an agent do the same, and then choose which one to hire.

Note: We don't have any meetings with the folks before any of these things. It's all about the work and the results.

content:
You have less than 6 days to try out this stealth model.

Ox Alpha just appeared on OpenRouter and OpenCode yesterday, and we still don’t know which lab or exact model is behind it.

Here’s what we know so far:

It’s free, has a 1M context window, supports text + image + video, and claims near unlimited usage with zero data retention.

There have been at least five previous stealth models released on the same platforms that were later claimed by Chinese labs. 

So I’d assume this one is almost certainly following the same playbook.

@davis7 ran early testing on a 10 task DeepSWE subset and the results already look ridiculous:

⟣  Ox Alpha: 80%

⟣  Fable5: 65%
⟣  GLM5.3: 62%
⟣  Grok4.6: 62%
⟣  GPT5.6-sol: 52%

These are still small sample sizes, but the gap is hard to ignore.

Plus if the technical fingerprints hold, this is most likely a https://t.co/6Ce1q5xfOV model; probably a multimodal upgrade sitting on top of the recent GLM5.3 stack.

And this matters because:

1. Iteration speed has become absurd:
 GLM5.3 itself came out only seven days earlier and was improved purely through internal post training and RL on the same base model. Meaning it had no new pre-training required.

2.  Holding back a strong model is becoming more expensive every month.

3.  The biggest pressure right now is on the closed labs. The gap is no longer measured in months, & in some areas it already feels like weeks.

I’ve been lazy asf about testing new models lately, but I’m getting on this one as soon as possible.

If you want to try it yourself:

> Head on to @OpenRouter: search for stealth/ox-alpha

Or go through @opencode (also free for the next few days)

GL anon.

title:
One thing I really like about OpenAI’s Private Safety Processing is that it doesn’t treat privacy and safety like they have to fight each other

With Zero Data Retention, customers already have a stro
content:
One thing I really like about OpenAI’s Private Safety Processing is that it doesn’t treat privacy and safety like they have to fight each other

With Zero Data Retention, customers already have a strong privacy setup

But there’s a problem with that approach as AI gets more powerful.

Some risks are impossible to understand from one prompt alone.

A user might slowly test the same safety limit across many requests, or an AI agent might start behaving differently after a long task

Looking at each interaction separately can miss the bigger picture

Private Safety Processing tries to solve that without giving OpenAI access to the actual customer content

The system can look for patterns across related activity, while OpenAI only gets a limited safety signal if something looks risky.

That part is important.
The goal isn't:
“Give OpenAI more data so they can make AI safer.”

It is:
“Find a way to improve safety while keeping customer data private.”

For companies working with financial data, health information, private research or sensitive business information, that difference matters a lot.

I think this is the direction AI safety needs to move toward.

More context for automated safety systems

Less access for humans

And more control for the customer

It’s still being tested, so the real test will be how well it works in practice.

But the idea itself is a meaningful step forward.

title:
In 1948, a 32-year-old at Bell Labs published a paper nobody fully understood.

Engineers found it too mathematical. Mathematicians found it too engineering-focused. One prominent mathematician review
content:
In 1948, a 32-year-old at Bell Labs published a paper nobody fully understood.

Engineers found it too mathematical. Mathematicians found it too engineering-focused. One prominent mathematician reviewed it negatively.

That paper - "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", became the founding document of the digital age.

The man was Claude Shannon. Father of Information Theory.

At 21, he wrote the most important master's thesis of the 20th century.

Working at MIT on an early mechanical computer, Shannon noticed its relay switches had exactly two states - open or closed. He had just taken a philosophy course introducing Boolean algebra, which also operated on two values: true and false.

Nobody had ever connected these two things.

His 1937 thesis proved that Boolean algebra and electrical circuits are mathematically identical, and that any logical operation could be built from simple switches.

Howard Gardner called it "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century."

Every digital computer ever built traces back to this insight.

At 29, he proved that perfect encryption exists.

During WWII, Shannon worked on classified cryptography at Bell Labs. His work contributed to SIGSALY, the secure voice system used for confidential communications between Roosevelt and Churchill.

In a classified 1945 memorandum, he mathematically proved the one-time pad provides perfect secrecy, unbreakable not just computationally, but provably, permanently, against an adversary with infinite power.

When declassified in 1949, it transformed cryptography from an art into a science. It laid the foundations for DES, AES, and every modern encryption standard.

At 32, he defined what information is.

His 1948 paper introduced one equation:
H = −Σ p(x) log p(x)

Shannon entropy. The average uncertainty in a probability distribution. The minimum bits required to encode a message.

Three things followed:

> He defined the bit - the fundamental unit of all information. His colleague John Tukey coined the name.

> He proved the channel capacity theorem, every communication channel has a maximum rate of reliable transmission. You can approach it. You can never exceed it.

> He unified telegraph, telephone, and radio into a single mathematical framework for the first time.

Robert Lucky of Bell Labs called it the greatest work "in the annals of technological thought."

Where his equation lives in AI today:

Cross-entropy loss - the function training every classifier and language model, is derived directly from H. Decision tree splits use information gain, which is H applied to data. Perplexity, the standard LLM evaluation metric, is an exponentiation of cross-entropy.

Every time a neural network trains, Shannon's formula runs inside it.

He also built the first AI learning device.

In 1950, Shannon built Theseus, a mechanical mouse that navigated a maze through trial and error, learned the correct path, and repeated it perfectly. Mazin Gilbert of Bell Labs said: "Theseus inspired the whole field of AI."

That same year he published the first paper on programming a computer to play chess. He co-organized the 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, the founding event of AI as a field.

The man:
He rode a unicycle through Bell Labs hallways while juggling. He built a flame-throwing trumpet, a rocket-powered Frisbee, and Styrofoam shoes to walk on the lake behind his house.

He called his home Entropy House.

When asked what motivated him: "I was motivated by curiosity. Never by the desire for financial gain. I just wondered how things were put together."

In 1985, he appeared unexpectedly at a conference in Brighton. The crowd mobbed him for autographs. Persuaded to speak at the banquet, he talked briefly, then pulled three balls from his pockets and juggled instead.

One engineer said: "It was as if Newton had showed up at a physics conference."

He died in 2001 after a decade with Alzheimer's, the cruel irony of information slowly leaving the mind of the man who defined what information was.

Claude, the AI model, is named after Claude Shannon, the mathematician who laid the foundation for the digital world we rely on today.

content:
Crypto spent 5 years defending itself from the same old attacks,,

And weirdly, three of the biggest ones are breaking at the same time.

Remember the old CT lines ::

"The US will kill crypto."

The SEC is now proposing actual rules for token raises, with paths for projects to raise and stay located.

"Stablecoins are backed by nothing."

@tether has moved from quarterly reserve attestations toward its first full Big Four financial audit with KPMG.

And my favorite one ::

"Crypto has no real use case except speculation."

Now look at what the biggest companies are building ::

--> @coinbase lets AI agents trade, pay and act within limits you set

--> @krakenfx is rebuilding its app with AI built into the product itself

--> @circle launched Agent Stack so agents can hold USDC, find services and pay onchain

The pattern is bigger than one headline ::

)- Regulation is moving from courtrooms  ->>rulebooks

)- Stablecoin proof is moving from snapshots ->>full audits

)- Crypto users are moving from only humans ->> software that can spend by itself

That last one matters the most.

For years crypto tried to convince normal people they needed programmable money.

AI agents do not need convincing.

They literally need money that software can use.

Crypto spent the last cycle asking ::

"How do we get the next billion humans onchain?"

The funny part is…

the next billion users might not be human at all.

For 5 years crypto had to explain why it should exist,,

Now the world is slowly building things that need it to exist. 👀

content:
🌍 INEDITUM Global Brief | August 21, 2026

THE ECONOMIC WAR AGAINST IRAN IS BECOMING A TEST OF CHINA’S ALIGNMENT

Good morning.

The most consequential development of the past 24 hours is Washington’s decision to escalate the Iran confrontation from sanctions against Tehran into a broader campaign aimed at forcing other economies to choose how they trade with Iran.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington is preparing what he described as the toughest sanctions campaign in history, explicitly calling on China and other countries to participate. Beijing has rejected the approach, arguing that additional sanctions will not resolve the conflict. The immediate target is Iran; the larger strategic test is whether Washington can persuade China to help enforce an economic blockade against a country that remains an important source of Chinese energy.

This creates a second front in the U.S.–China relationship. The dispute is no longer confined to tariffs, semiconductors or AI. Energy access, sanctions enforcement and financial connectivity are now entering the bilateral contest.

Oil markets are responding accordingly. Brent has moved back toward $94 a barrel, reflecting renewed concern that the disruption around Hormuz will persist. The important issue is no longer simply how much oil is physically unavailable. It is whether governments and companies can reliably determine which cargoes, banks, insurers and routes will remain politically usable.

The pressure is also reaching Europe’s energy security. Romania scrambled F-16s after a drone approached the area of the Neptun Deep gas project in the Black Sea, highlighting the growing security exposure of new European energy infrastructure. The project is strategically important because Romania expects it to become a major source of regional gas supply.

Meanwhile, global bond markets remain under pressure. The U.S. 30-year Treasury yield has returned to around 5.25%, despite Washington’s attempts to contain long-term borrowing costs. Higher yields are now interacting directly with elevated energy prices and government deficits, increasing the cost of financing across advanced economies.

China is therefore facing a particularly difficult strategic calculation.

Supporting Washington’s Iran campaign could help restore energy-market stability and maritime trade.

Resisting it protects Beijing’s economic relationship with Tehran and reinforces China’s position against unilateral U.S. sanctions.

Either choice carries a cost.

STRATEGIC ASSESSMENT

The important change is that economic neutrality is becoming harder to maintain.

For years, China, India, Gulf economies and other middle powers could preserve commercial relationships across competing geopolitical blocs.

The Iran crisis is testing whether that model still works when the United States attempts to turn sanctions compliance into a condition of access to the Western financial system.

The emerging competition is therefore no longer simply:

Who controls the technology?

It is becoming:

Who controls the economic network through which the technology, energy and capital move?

WHY IT MATTERS

For companies, this creates a new form of geopolitical exposure.

A country does not have to be under sanctions itself to become vulnerable.

Its banks, shipping companies, insurers, energy suppliers or trading partners can become the pressure points.

The strategic advantage will increasingly belong to companies capable of maintaining multiple routes to capital, energy, technology and markets without becoming dependent on a single geopolitical system.

EXECUTIVE QUESTION

If Washington and Beijing turn economic alignment into a condition of market access, can your business remain genuinely neutral?

content:
i wish more people in ai just found the models intrinsically interesting without an agenda.

i remember back when i was embedded in the linguistics crowd, i was very confused why nobody i talked to seemed to find deep learning or later GPT-3 interesting. don't these people care about language understanding and linguistic production? so why are they ignoring and dismissing this?

eventually i gave up and found tpot and the rationalists and mechinterp and everything i do now, and it's - to be clear - much better. but i still sometimes look around and see so many people doing research because they care about safety and x-risk, or steering capabilities because they want the singularity to go well, or posting blog posts about ai pause because they're worried about doom, or grinding gpu kernels or yelling at claude in a loop because they want to escape the permanent underclass...

those are all well and good, i can respect (at least some of) those motivations, and many of them intersect with finding the models at least instrumentally interesting - but i really just find the models interesting, terminally. it's what got me into this, and everything else is kind of a side project. i just want to know how and why the models do what they do.

i'm not without my Theories and my biases - it especially frustrates me how, per @norvid_studies, "people get used to anything in two weeks" and start kvetching about things that a few years ago would have been Fantastic Science Fiction - but ultimately, when i write, it's coming from a place of wonder about how these things work.

content:
Code reviews still remain to be the largest bottleneck for me. It’s gone up significantly more as Goals become a core part of my workflow.

I’m not quiet there for rubber stamping everything yet like some engineers especially for code that’s going out to billions of users but here are some high level strats that’s been working for me reduce review time.

1. I think of code as a tree. Leaf nodes are code with new dependencies. Think of some new component code. Trunk code is infra code changes that touches a lot of stuff. How deeply I review code slides in depth depending on how close to the trunk it is.

2. Anchor on safety and leverage feature gating. I’ve been preferring forking dangerous code and quickly cleaning up after A/B testing the infra changes. I also just gate everything I can.

3. Leverage adversarial agent reviews with my own rules. agents can cheat if you tell it to review code in the same thread the code was written in. It’s needs a clean context

4. Have good diff or PR writing rules. Same good eng practices still apply. Small, atomic diffs with good test plans and summary. Don’t make giant summaries that are longer than the lines of code change 😭

5. Don’t be so nit picky. The era of code as artistic expression is over. Be okay that the AI didn’t write the code in your favorite way.

In the end, I still read every diff but how sometimes I skim depending on the safety scale. The above rules help me quickly anchor on the level of effort I need to spend

Hope this helps. I’m pretty sure I missed some tips lol.

Every LLM query doesn’t need your biggest, most expensive model.

LLMRouter is an open-source library for builders who want to route each query to a suitable LLM instead of sending every task to one default model.

It helps you balance response quality and inference cost by selecting models according to task complexity, cost, and performance requirements.

Key features:

• 16+ routing methods – experiment with KNN, SVM, MLP, matrix factorization, Elo, graph-based routing, and more
• Five routing categories – covers single-round, multi-round, multimodal, agentic, and personalized routing
• Unified CLI – train routers, run inference, or launch an interactive Gradio chat interface
• Data generation pipeline – build routing data from 11 benchmark datasets with API calling and evaluation
• Extensible workflow – add custom routers and task definitions through documented plugin systems

It’s open-source (MIT license).

How to build great evals - part 4

The reason enterprises struggle with building decent AI systems is the lack of an eval strategy.

You need a laddered eval strategy, for your unique use cases,
with multiple evals on the cost/realism spectrum.

Here are the key kinds of evals you need:

Hill-climb long evals : this pushes the frontier of your product and you need to continually refresh this to improve quality and expand your feature base.

Regression evals : Did we break the product of today while hill climbing?

Smoke test evals: safety and the absolute basics that just can’t go wrong. Not necessarily hard questions, but important to not get wrong. Eg product identity.

Launch evals: often close to an online test with real-ish traffic. Less control, but the most realistic.

More in tomorrow’s post!

title:
⚡️The long-run containment strategy is going to fail.

That is the real answer.

Once frontier-level intelligence becomes compressible enough to run on commodity hardware, capability becomes informati
content:
⚡️The long-run containment strategy is going to fail.

That is the real answer.

Once frontier-level intelligence becomes compressible enough to run on commodity hardware, capability becomes information, and information is extraordinarily difficult to recall after diffusion. 

Model weights can be copied perfectly, encrypted, mirrored globally, modified privately, distilled into smaller descendants, and preserved indefinitely.

There is no stable world where humanity simultaneously gets rapidly advancing AI and permanently keeps every dangerous capability behind the APIs of a handful of compliant companies.

That world disappears as models become smaller.

And this changes the Dario/Sacks debate substantially.

If governments construct an elaborate permission system around frontier labs while comparable capabilities diffuse into local models shortly afterward, they risk regulating the actors easiest to regulate while progressively losing control over the actors they actually fear.

That creates a perverse equilibrium:

the compliant frontier becomes permissioned while the uncontrollable frontier becomes underground.

The capability keeps moving.

The visibility disappears.

That is worse.

There will still be capabilities worth delaying at the frontier, especially genuinely catastrophic biological, cyber, autonomous replication, or weapons capabilities. Months of lead time can be enormously valuable.

But permanent containment cannot be the foundation.

The durable architecture has to assume:

powerful intelligence eventually becomes abundant, private, cheap, and impossible to centrally revoke.

Once that assumption is accepted, the entire safety problem changes.

You harden biological synthesis.

You harden critical infrastructure.

You redesign cybersecurity around machine-speed attackers and defenders.

You secure dangerous physical inputs.

You improve attribution.

You build AI systems whose job is detecting and neutralizing malicious AI activity.

You move defenses closer to the physical chokepoints where digital instructions become real-world consequences.

Essentially:

Stop assuming dangerous cognition can remain scarce. Build a world capable of surviving abundant cognition.

And there is an even deeper consequence.

Alignment itself becomes competitive.

If one person has an unrestricted model capable of generating an attack, millions of defenders can eventually have models capable of recognizing that attack, patching vulnerabilities, detecting anomalous behavior, designing countermeasures, and responding at machine speed.

So the equilibrium does not have to be “one malicious person gets superintelligence and civilization ends.”

It can become machine offense versus machine defense, with humans governing the infrastructure underneath both.

That infrastructure becomes the real battlefield.

Compute.

Networks.

DNA synthesis.

Robotics.

Energy.

Identity.

Financial rails.

Physical access.

The bits eventually need atoms.

And atoms still have chokepoints.

That is where enforceable safety migrates.

content:
George Soros and the Open Society Foundations – The Capillary System.

Everyone says Soros this, Soros that. But how do they actually operate?

Most of the organizations we have described operate at the elite level – the meeting in Davos, the seminar and the committee in Brussels. The Open Society Foundations are different. They operate at every level simultaneously – from the supranational to the local, from the think tank to the street activist, from the Supreme Court brief to the district attorney election. The most complete political funding infrastructure ever built by a private individual.
Follow the money – most of it is hiding in plain sight.

Soros made his fortune speculating on national currencies – most famously breaking the British Pound in 1992. He used the proceeds to fund institutions that argue against national sovereignties, helping him make such operations. This is not irony. It is a business model. An arbitrage.

1. The mechanism is simple and almost elegant. You create a nicely named organization – an institute for open society, a foundation for democratic media, a center for justice reform. You seed it with ten million dollars of private money, enough to hire staff, produce reports, and establish credibility. Then, through the network of associates and ideologically aligned officials that decades of funding have placed inside governments and supranational bodies, you ensure that this private organization receives hundreds of millions in public funding – EU grants, USAID contracts, government subsidies. The private money creates the platform. The public hundreds of millions buy the reach. The taxpayer funds the project. The project serves the agenda.
A nice arbitrage again.

2. Let’s imagine in every country a main foundation operating as a buzzing corporate office — a headquarters — populated with people who know the agenda best and understand how it connects to the global program. Everyone comes there for instructions. Every smaller organization in the country — the migration NGO, the media fund, the arts prize committee — knows where to come for orientation, for funding, for the framing of the next campaign. It looks like a civil society hub. The people inside it may believe they are doing good. The architecture ensures that doing good means advancing the agenda.

3. The network controls the full loop. The think tank produces the paper. The advocacy group runs the campaign. The legal organization takes it to court. The media organization covers it favorably. The fact-checker delegitimizes the opposition. Each may look independent; the funding architecture connects them. The public annual reports list the grants and recipients. The architecture is not hidden. It is simply too layered for most people to read clearly.

4. The cultural layer is the most insidious. The network funds literary prizes that go to authors advancing the agenda. They fund film festivals, journalism awards, university chairs. None of this requires explicit editorial control. You don’t tell the prize committee who to select. You fund the prize committee. Over time the selection reflects the values of the funder.

5. In America, Soros-backed political groups have funded progressive prosecutors and district-attorney campaigns. The money is visible in campaign-finance records; the resulting policies are visible in the cities where they were implemented.

6. In Europe, the same architecture appears around migration: advocacy organizations, legal challenges, NGOs, political lobbying, and media narratives. The different pieces reinforce one another. One source. Every layer. Taxpayer money amplifying private money at every stage.

7. That is the capillary system: an ideological project reaching from elite institutions down into everyday life. The activist, journalist, lawyer, academic, official, and politician do not need to know one another or consciously share a master plan. Networks, institutions, and funding create the coordination.

“Observe” feels harmless and innocuous, almost passive. In reality, AI labs actively bypass all safety measures in order to extract all data they can at any cost, obviously ignoring crawler directives, but also impersonating users, engaging in deceptive behavior, and proactively implementing workarounds to any new protection measure you set to try to keep the boat afloat and safeguard your users. title:
Lots here. It's a wake-up call. Well worth a listen

Barry Appleton, professor specializing in international negotiations & trade, discussed the prolonged meeting between Canadian and U.S. officials.
content:
Lots here. It's a wake-up call. Well worth a listen

Barry Appleton, professor specializing in international negotiations & trade, discussed the prolonged meeting between Canadian and U.S. officials. The talks, expected to last about 30 minutes, stretched into a third hour. Appleton viewed this positively:
“Well, of course it’s good news because at the end of the day, the goal here is to get some certainty, is to try to get some type of agreement. Basically, Canada has paid. We don’t know what they paid, but they paid for a three day sort of delay on these massive tariffs. So you want to get your money’s worth. If we paid for three days, I want to get some value for it. Having three hours of meeting rather than 45 minutes of meeting has got to be a good thing rather than a bad thing.”

He framed the situation as an “extractive exercise” by the US, noting Canada previously surrendered the digital services tax (DST) with nothing in return. Key missing protections he highlighted were a “standstill” (no new tariffs) and a “snapback” (automatic penalty if other side breaks terms). Canada lacks both, unlike Mexico

Appleton criticized the Canadian government’s secrecy—contrasting it with Mexico’s transparent daily agendas and official readouts—saying this leaves Canadians anxious and swinging between optimism and pessimism:
“Right now, Canadians don’t know. So we’re worried, we’re anxious. You see this everywhere. And we swing. We swing either too optimistic or too pessimistic because we have imperfect information. That was a choice by the Canadian government. I think it’s a poor choice.”

Appleton argued greater transparency and clear signaling improve outcomes, not secrecy. Softwood lumber (a 44-year dispute) appeared sidelined, raising concerns for provinces like British Columbia. He noted premiers control key concessions (e.g., ending the U.S. booze ban) and lack a proper federal-provincial trade council structure, creating internal Canadian problems:
“Our problem is structure. So much of this is our own problems. It’s sort of like in FIFA, in the World cup, if we’re scoring on our own net…”

On the broader picture and CUSMA, Appleton stated:
“So first of all, CUSMA as we know it, according to Premier Mo today is dead. Okay, so CUSMA is there. It’s a foundational agreement, could be terminated on six months notice. Donald Trump doesn’t have to give us a reason. Obviously we want the CUSMA to continue.”

He described the current talks as temporary “surge pricing” or “paying for parking” to delay big tariffs, likely leading to a reciprocal trade deal (an “ART”) rather than restoring free access. Canadians should prepare for the end of free market access to the U.S., with baseline tariffs possibly in the 10–15% range (similar to UK/EU/Japan deals) on everything, plus sectoral issues (steel, aluminum, autos, lumber). 

Digital/AI alignment and other concessions appear already underway without public consultation. Finally, he urged focus on Canadian innovation and productivity, better federal-provincial coordination, and greater public transparency @bappleton

content:
Four cities. Four icons. One visual language.

GPT Image 2

Prompt:
Create a refined 3:4 vertical premium travel poster for [CITY].

First identify the city, country, architecture, landscape, climate, cultural character, and visual identity. Select ONE iconic and highly recognizable real-world landmark or subject as the HERO. Establish one believable photographic viewpoint and ensure every environmental element logically belongs to that location. Do not create a collage of unrelated landmarks.

COMPOSITION: Divide the poster into two perfectly equal sections: 50% top and 50% bottom. Use a warm beige, ivory, or soft-white background with generous negative space and precise alignment.

TOP — HERO PHOTOGRAPH: Create an ultra-realistic, high-end editorial photograph of the chosen landmark from a believable real-world viewpoint. Preserve accurate architecture, proportions, materials, surrounding environment, natural lighting, shadows, atmosphere, and geographic character. The scene should feel like premium architectural photography or a museum-quality travel photograph, with realistic textures and sophisticated cinematic composition.

BOTTOM — GRAPHIC INTERPRETATION: Reinterpret the same hero landmark as a sophisticated flat graphic design. Extract its most recognizable silhouette, contours, structural details, proportions, and distinctive architectural elements. Simplify them into elegant geometric shapes, flat color blocks, thin lines, restrained divisions, and generous negative space. The landmark must remain instantly recognizable without becoming a realistic illustration, 3D render, cartoon, or game graphic.

COLOR & TYPOGRAPHY: Derive a restrained palette of approximately 4–6 colors from the city's architecture, environment, and hero photograph. Keep the palette sophisticated with slightly muted saturation. Add minimal geometric accents only when they improve the composition.

Use limited, elegant typography such as: [CITY] [COUNTRY] ARCHITECTURAL STUDY 2026

Use Swiss/international graphic design, architectural exhibition posters, luxury editorial design, and museum visual identity as the aesthetic reference. Keep typography subtle, with generous letter spacing and strong visual hierarchy.

FINAL AESTHETIC: Sophisticated, minimal, contemporary, culturally authentic, artistic, and premium. The photographic upper half and graphic lower half should feel like two expressions of the same visual identity. The final result should resemble a world-class gallery poster, collector's travel print, architectural exhibition artwork, or luxury brand campaign.

Avoid landmark collages, inaccurate architecture, invented structures, excessive text, tourist-brochure aesthetics, neon, flashy effects, heavy gradients, glossy 3D rendering, cartoon styling, game UI, clutter, excessive decoration, and generic AI-generated cityscapes.

𝟵 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀:

𝟭. 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲
• Stores those embeddings for fast semantic retrieval

𝟮. 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
• Transforms text into numerical vectors that carry meaning
• The foundation for everything retrieval-related. Your choice here 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 of everything downstream

𝟯. 𝗥𝗔𝗚
• Query, retrieve relevant context, generate a grounded answer
• The standard fix for a model that doesn't know your data
• Most RAG failures are 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀, not generation failures

𝟰. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴

• 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 in the stack, and still the first thing to try before adding infrastructure

𝟱. 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲
• Look up whether a semantically similar query was already answered. Hit means serve the cached response, miss means call the model
• The 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 available. Real user traffic contains far more near-duplicate questions than teams expect

𝟲. 𝗠𝗖𝗣
• Connects models to external data, tools, and services through 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹
• Turns integration from bespoke glue into a standard interface

𝟳. 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
• Goal, memory, planning, action
• Function calling gives it 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀. Memory gives it 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗶𝘁𝘆. Planning is what makes it an agent rather than a tool call

𝟴. 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴
• The model decides which API or tool to invoke, and with what arguments
• This is the 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁. MCP standardises where those functions live

𝟵. 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀
• User input passes through policies and rules before and after the model, producing safe output
• The layer that decides whether any of the above is 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀

content:
Codexが最近リミット到達すんの早くね？
利用上限絞った？に対するTiboさんの回答

「文句言ってる人調べたら、多くの人がsub2api使ってたよ」

【sub2apiとは？】

簡単にいうと、
ChatGPT/Codexの月額サブスクを、普通のAPIみたいに変換して使えるようにする中継サーバー。

しかも単なる個人用の変換ツールではなく、複数アカウントをまとめたり、独自のAPIキーを発行したり、複数ユーザーに配ったり、課金までできる仕組みを持っている。

イメージすると、

ChatGPT Proを月額で契約
↓
その利用枠をsub2apiに食わせる
↓
OpenAI APIっぽい入口を作る
↓
他のツールや複数人から大量に使う

って感じ。

Tiboさんが言っているのは
「サブスクの利用枠をAPI化して、再配布したり多数のユーザーで共有したりする使い方はサポートしていない。そのような通信は不正利用防止システムに検知される」
ってことだけど、じゃあサードパーティ製クライアント使うのダメなの？っていうとそういうことではなくて、Tiboさん自身

- 公式Codex
- Pi
- OpenCode
- その他「Sign in with ChatGPT」に対応したオープンソース製クライアント

については、自分のChatGPTアカウントでログインして自分のサブスク枠を使うなら問題ないと明言してる。

なので境界線は
- 自分1人がChatGPT認証で別クライアントを使う → OK
- サブスクをAPIサーバー化して再配布・共有・販売する → NG

要は正規の使い方してない人達はサポート対象外だよってことなんだけど、このポストには大量の

「いやsub2apiなんか使ってないけど普通に上限明らかに少なくなってるわ！！！」

という大量のリプがついていて、絶賛物議を醸しているよ。

って感じです。

content:
会社のピンチを、次の事業に変えます。
本日、新サービス
「AIクリエイターCAMP」をローンチします。

会社がピンチだと知ったとき、ヒカルさんが連絡をくれました。
「何かできることはないか」と、本気で助けようとしてくれました。
一番苦しいタイミングで差し伸べてもらった手を、僕は忘れません。林さんや桑田さんをはじめ他にも色々な方が声をかけてくれました。
本当にありがとうございます。

貸付金を含む問題が解決したわけではありません。
必要なことには引き続き向き合いますが、これ以上、誰かに対して強い言葉を重ねたいとも思っていません。
これからは、事業と結果で前に進んでいることを伝えていきます。

これから間違いなく、大AI時代が来ます。
その中でAIクリエイターは、AIに触れ、その可能性を実感するための最も入りやすい入口の一つです。

サムライパートナーズ、そしてByteDanceにも関わっていただき、動画生成AI「Seedance」を実際に使いながら学べる専用プラットフォームを用意しました。
ByteDanceの協力のもと作り上げたスクールとしては、初の取り組みです。

ただ、AIクリエイターCAMPは終点ではありません。
まずは、成果が目に見えて分かりやすい「AIで動画を作ること」から始める。
そこから、さまざまなAIを組み合わせ、仕事を効率化したり、事業の課題を解決したりできる力へと広げていく。
最終的には、企業や個人の課題に対して「どのAIを、どう使えば解決できるか」を提案し、実行までできる。
いわば、AIコンサルタントのような人材を育てたいと考えています。
その最初の入口が、AIクリエイターCAMPです。

動画編集CAMPも、これまで積み上げてきたものにAIを掛け合わせ、第二章が始まっています。
弟が残したものを守るだけではなく、そのレガシーを引き継ぎながら、新しい時代に必要なものをつくっていく。

これが、会社を立て直すための最初の一歩です。
これからAIを学びたい方も、動画編集者として次の武器を持ちたい方も、ここから始めてください。

content:
Codexのおかけで1日50本以上の
ロング動画を生成してSNS伸ばしまくってます
CapCatやPremiere Proはもう3ヶ月以上使ってない　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　

動画編集において
1カットずつ調整する必要がなくなり始めてる

やることは、Codexに
「こんな動画を作って」
と伝えるだけ。
するとAIが、
・企画、脚本を作成
・ストーリーボードを設計
・必要な素材を用意
・ナレーションを生成
・字幕を作成
・カット、テンポを編集
・最終レンダリング

ここまで一気に進めてくれる。

さらに面白いのが、
「参考動画」を渡したとき。

動画の内容をそのままコピーするのではなく、
・脚本の構成
・冒頭のフック
・ショットの切り替え
・映像のテンポ
・ビジュアルの方向性
などを分析して
それを参考に別の動画案を作らせることもできる。

試すならCodexにこれを入力
👇
「OpenMontageを使って、10〜15秒のAIツール紹介動画を作ってください。
まず最適な動画制作ワークフローを分析し、脚本、ストーリーボード、素材、ナレーション、字幕、編集、最終レンダリングまで自動で完了してください。

最初の3秒には強力なフックを入れ、全体はテンポを速めに。字幕はスマホ視聴でも読みやすいサイズ・長さにしてください。

重要ではない判断は自律的に行い、レンダリング後に字幕、映像と音声の同期、異常なフレームがないかチェックしてください。
問題を発見した場合は自動修正し、再レンダリングして完成版を出力してください。」

これだけ。

「AIに動画を作らせる」から、
企画 → 制作 → 編集 → 品質チェック → 修正
までAIに回させる時代になった

動画編集も自動化したいなら
8月23日にリリースするCodexの教科書を
読んでセッティングしちゃって
詳しくは👇

・長年にわたり、職場の膨大な会話履歴を組織の知識へと変換することは不可能だった
・しかし、AIエージェントの登場によってその情報の整理と活用が可能に

・Slack上のClaudeが要約や準備
content:
SlackがAIエージェントといかに協働しているか、というAnthropicの記事。個人的に好みで、この方向は強いと思っている。

・長年にわたり、職場の膨大な会話履歴を組織の知識へと変換することは不可能だった
・しかし、AIエージェントの登場によってその情報の整理と活用が可能に

・人間とエージェントの働き方の基本リズムは、タスクの引き継ぎサイクルにある
・Slack上のClaudeが要約や準備などの作業を行い、人間がレビューして意思決定を下す
・毎朝のブリーフィングや会議の準備などは、エージェントに任せるのに最適なタスク

・エージェントは1対1のチャットボットではなく、同僚のように扱うアプローチが良い
・人間のチームメンバーと同じように、明確な目標や特定の担当領域を持たせる
・ユーザーが明確な価値を実感できないエージェントは、引退させるべきタイミング

・チャンネルは原則publicとし、privateにするのは明確な理由がある時のみにとどめる
・エージェントは見えるものからしか学べないから
・公開されたコンテキストが蓄積し、エージェントの知恵となって人間に還元されていく
・ただ、そのためには作成途中の案でも安心して共有できる環境は欠かせない（PrivateやDMが使われるのは気まずいから）

・新しい働き方を浸透させるには、チームメンバーの実践を直接見るのが一番早い
・社内全体でワークフローやプロンプトのコツを共有するチャンネルを立ち上げる
・他の人がコピーできる文書を残すことで、誰かの一工夫がチームのテンプレートになる

・トークン使用量のような活動指標は導入の目安にすぎず、成果の証明にはならない
・AI導入によるビジネス価値を測るには、ダッシュボードではなく独自の判断基準が必要
・既存の仕事を単に高速化するのではなく、働き方そのものをチームで再構築していく

（たまたまだけど、昨日の #SHIFT_EVOLVE で似た話をしていた）

content:
$PLTR New article | “Palantir cashes in on paranoia as bosses swap Hamptons for bootcamp” | Including comments from @chadwahl 

“Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir Technologies, acknowledged on Wednesday the paranoia of business leaders who were choosing to spend a hot day in August at a software bootcamp in Manhattan, while “bankers are in the Hamptons, explaining to us how the world should work”. 
…
“Karp told a room full of executives from nearly 100 companies on Wednesday: they’d better make sure that their “alpha does not leave your building and end up in a competitor’s hands or in a company that will someday compete and try to kill you”.
________________________________________

“Chad Wahlquist (@chadwahl), forward deployed architect at Palantir, said he does not think the AI labs are taking enterprise data “exactly” from a company’s prompts and turning on them as competitors.

Instead, he said businesses are suspicious about the incentives of AI labs, including those that are asking customers, in some cases, to pay more to have zero data retention, “not because the zero data retention costs more money”, but because “they don’t have access to your data” for training models.

He added: “You look at this from multiple different angles, like, what are they [the frontier labs] trying to do? Then they’re opening up, hey, Claude Science, OpenAI for science.” Businesses are thinking, according to Wahlquist: “Wait, I’m
competing with this. How are they getting this intelligence? What are they doing?” … 
“Why do I want to fund someone that’s going to be a competitor to me?”

content:
Small but important correction: these are NOT "open source AI".

Genuinely permissive on the released weights and code: DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2, Meituan LongCat-2.0, and Ant's Ling-3.0-flash and Ring-2.6-1T are MIT. Tencent Hy3 is Apache 2.0.

The rest ship custom licenses with commercial triggers.

- MiniMax M3 uses the MiniMax Community License, where the base grant is non-commercial. Commercial use requires displaying "Built with MiniMax M3," and above $20M yearly revenue you need prior written authorization.

- Kimi K3 requires a separate agreement with Moonshot if you operate a Model-as-a-Service business and the aggregate revenue of you and your affiliates crosses $20M over any consecutive 12 months.

- Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B uses the same structure at $50M, scoped to MaaS and AI work assistant businesses.

Kimi and Qwen both add attribution requirements above 100M MAU or $20M monthly revenue.

And the distinction people keep skipping: an MIT or Apache license on weights does NOT make the system open source.

The @OpenSourceOrg definition requires the preferred form for modifying the system, meaning parameters, complete training and inference code, and sufficient information about the training data to substantially reproduce it.

Nothing on this list clears that bar.

title:
NEW METHOD TO TRAIN ROBOTS: Physical Intelligence is at it again!

Not so new actually, but worth mentioning because its impact is still going strong today.

Called Real-Time Action Chunking (RTC), it
content:
NEW METHOD TO TRAIN ROBOTS: Physical Intelligence is at it again!

Not so new actually, but worth mentioning because its impact is still going strong today.

Called Real-Time Action Chunking (RTC), it is an inference-time method from Physical Intelligence @physical_int for running flow and diffusion-based vision-language-action models in real time.

A few definitions:
- Action chunk: a short block of future actions (say the next 50 motor commands) predicted in one shot instead of one step at a time.
- Flow matching: a faster cousin of diffusion -> the model learns a straight-line path from noise to the target action trajectory, so it needs only a few integration steps instead of many denoising ones.
- Diffusion: a generative method that starts from pure noise and iteratively denoises it into structured output. Here, the output is a trajectory of robot actions rather than an image.
- Inpainting: the image-editing trick where a generative model fills in a masked region so it's consistent with the pixels around it. Diffusion and flow models can do this natively. RTC's insight is that a chunk of robot actions can be "inpainted" the same way: freeze the part already committed, generate the rest to match.
- Inference-time method: a change to how the trained model is used, not how it's trained: no new data, no fine-tuning, no architecture change.
- Closed-loop control: act, observe the result, correct, continuously. The opposite of executing a pre-planned motion blind. "Synchronous closed-loop at 10 Hz" means the robot would have to pause and wait for each new decision, which is exactly the stutter RTC removes. 

A chunked VLA predicts a block of future actions, then has to compute the next block while still executing the current one.
Naively switching to the freshly computed chunk mid-motion results in disaster because the new actions conflict with the trajectory in progress, producing jerks and pauses that aren't in the training data.

RTC frames the handoff as an inpainting problem: the actions that will execute before the next inference arrives are frozen to the previous chunk's values, and the model inpaints the remaining actions under partial attention, using the native inpainting ability of flow/diffusion samplers.
It requires no training-time changes and runs on existing models (π0, π0.5, π0-FAST), demonstrated on match-striking, Ethernet-cable insertion and clothing folding.

The whole method is a reframe: treat real-time control as inpainting.
Diffusion and flow VLAs can already inpaint (fill masked outputs conditioned on known ones), so RTC just freezes the actions that will execute before the next inference lands and lets the model inpaint the rest without any training-time changes.
That means any existing flow/diffusion VLA gets smooth async execution for free: no new data, no fine-tune, no architecture change.
The latency problem is solved entirely at sampling time by borrowing a capability the models already had.

Typical remote inference is 108ms (static) to 139ms (mobile) total, including 97ms of model inference.
Roughly 100ms per decision is about 10Hz, far too slow for smooth synchronous closed-loop control, so a big VLA physically cannot "stop, think, act" without visible pauses.

The evaluation metric is throughput: proportion of substeps completed successfully divided by duration, and the tasks are ones where a mistimed pause is catastrophic.
Match-striking needs a continuous stroke, cable insertion needs steady precision, folding needs uninterrupted motion.
PI chose tasks where discontinuity ruins the attempt, which is exactly where RTC's benefit is most visible.
The metric rewards both success and speed at once.

title:

It’s not simply about collecting more robot data.

content:
The more I look into @axisrobotics  the more I understand what they mean by a “compounding data engine.”

It’s not simply about collecting more robot data.

The interesting part is how each cycle makes the next one more valuable.

Axis brings together simulation, teleoperation, and real-world robot interaction to build the data needed to train robot policies.

But training the policy is only the beginning.

The policy goes back into the real world and tries to perform the task.

Sometimes it gets it right.

Sometimes it doesn’t.

When it fails, a human steps in and provides the correct behavior.

That correction doesn’t just fix one attempt.

It becomes new training data.

The improved policy goes back out, encounters new situations, and creates another round of useful feedback.

So the loop becomes:

Simulation = Teleoperation = Data = Policy = Deployment = Failure = Correction = Better Data = Better Policy

And then it repeats.

That’s the part I find most interesting about Axis.

The goal isn’t to build a massive dataset and leave it there.

It’s to create a system where the performance of the current policy helps determine what data should be collected next.

Every failure becomes informative.

Every correction can improve the next policy.

Every better policy can reach situations the previous one couldn’t handle.

Over time, the dataset isn’t just getting bigger.

It’s getting more relevant.

And that’s why I think the “compounding” part matters.

The real advantage may not be the amount of data Axis has collected.

It’s the feedback loop connecting data, policies, robots, and human expertise and making every cycle build on the one before it.

That’s a very interesting way to think about scaling robot learning.

content:
Unconfirmed: Optimus already Operating in a Test Environment at 🇩🇪 Giga Berlin

According to a media report, the management of the Tesla Gigafactory in Grünheide officially confirmed to select media representatives on August 21, 2026, that the company’s humanoid robot, known as "Optimus," has begun initial test runs at the Brandenburg plant.

I was unable to find independent confirmation of the report; however, given that employees at Giga Berlin begin generating training data for Optimus in August and the plant manager stated in an interview a few weeks ago that manufacturing Optimus in Berlin was a possibility the report could well be accurate.

The report states: "In a targeted communication to select press representatives, including hh-autos. com, Tesla specified that several units of the robot's second generation (Gen 2) have been deployed since the beginning of the week in isolated areas of battery cell production and internal logistics."

According to the report, the Optimus units are handling the sorting, inspection, and loading of cell carriers. The core focus of this initial trial phase in Germany is the handling of the new 4680 battery cells. Equipped with advanced sensor technology and an end-to-end control system based on FSD hardware, the Optimus units are tasked with sorting, inspecting, and loading cell carriers.

The report states: "The confirmation from Grünheide on the morning of August 21, 2026, did not come as a surprise to industry insiders, though the precision of the details did. Unlike earlier announcements, which often remained vague, Tesla clearly defined the deployment location and the scope of the task. The tests are not taking place in the actual final assembly area for the Model Y but are instead focusing on two strategically important and highly automated areas: the newly ramped-up production of 4680 battery cells and the adjacent plant logistics. According to the statement, this is a 'limited pilot trial to evaluate system stability and human-machine interaction in a real-world production environment.'"

We should treat the report with caution until we receive further confirmation, but there is a valid probability that it is accurate.

title: 🪸 [Call for contributors!] 🪸 New release: "Google Docs for Coral Reefs" is live!! You can now explore the reef with your dive buddies, select coral colonies, tag species, add comments, and search for
content:
🪸 [Call for contributors!] 🪸 New release: "Google Docs for Coral Reefs" is live!! You can now explore the reef with your dive buddies, select coral colonies, tag species, add comments, and search for visually similar colonies across the reef, all in 3D!

🔵 Why? Coral reefs are such precious, beautiful, incredibly complex, and threatened ecosystems. They are dying fast. A lot of amazing people are fighting to keep them alive. We need to deploy more solutions faster. That requires a deep understanding of how coral reefs function. What works, what doesn't, to coordinate precise action. The evidence is buried in a humongous amount of data scattered across organisations, hard drives, and disconnected tools. We need one place to share the data, examine it, analyse it, and turn it into action. That’s why we’re building this!

🔵 Ground truth is everything. We start with the highest-signal data: time-series 3D. You see each colony from many angles, at true scale, and track how it evolves over time. But the data is enormous. Even small survey plots are hundreds of gigabytes. We already process and stream it directly in the browser. Now we turn it into a workspace.

🔵 Dive buddies. Annotating hectares of reef is soo lonely. So we built multiplayer! Bring your friends and annotate together in 3D. See where everyone is looking in real time and split up the work. Leave comments at exact locations. Use @ tags for species, health, etc. Pretty much like Google Docs or Figma, but for a 3D reef.

🔵 Smart selection. Corals are painfully hard to annotate! Their shapes and colours are all different, and it's hard to see where one colony ends and another begins. Even amazing 2D models like SAM struggle with reef photos and orthos. Lousy masks and vague point annotations create bad training data. Those errors wreck downstream AI models. Luckily, we have an unfair advantage. Each coral appears in many photos from different angles. Our selector works in a shared 3D embedding space, across every view at once. Just Shift+click, drag out a semantic radius, and select anything directly in 3D.

🔵 Semantic search. Start with a colony, coral fragment, or disease patch. Hit the ≈ button and find visually similar things across the reef. Create a category and add the right matches. Keep going until you’ve mapped it. Then move on to the next one.

🔵 Under the hood. We project DINOv3 features from the photos into the 3D splats. Then we use LDA to adapt them to your categories and make the model lightweight enough to work in the browser.

🔵 Please break it. This demo is one tiny patch of reef, held together with duct tape and full of bugs. But even in this state, no other browser tool lets a team annotate a 3D reef together like this.

🔵 Huge thanks to the superstar Matthew Osborne, creator of The Living Atlas, for leading the development! The fantastic Jan Paulini built our first species list. And to the amazing people doing the real work in the water, who kindly shared this reef data with us:  
@alderdice_r,  @reefgenomics, @emmafcamp,  
@PaigeStrudwick,  
@ChristineDRoper, and many others.

🔵 Please annotate a few colonies. It would help us a lot! Together, we map every reef on Earth! 🤗 🌍

title:
A robotics dataset can contain thousands of successful demonstrations and still teach a model a surprisingly narrow world.

The reason is simple: success count and experience coverage are different th
content:
A robotics dataset can contain thousands of successful demonstrations and still teach a model a surprisingly narrow world.

The reason is simple: success count and experience coverage are different things.

That is why the Task Generation layer at @axisrobotics deserves more attention than it usually gets.

Axis can vary a task across several dimensions before contributors ever touch the controls: the robot embodiment, objects involved, spatial arrangement, semantics, and visual conditions. Its task pipeline also uses randomized object poses, clutter configurations, and camera viewpoints while preserving the underlying objective.

So two contributors may technically perform the same skill while generating meaningfully different training situations.

Consider grasping. Repeating one grasp thousands of times from nearly identical positions mostly increases density around an experience the model already has. Change the object's pose, surrounding clutter, viewpoint, or scene configuration and the model has to solve the same underlying capability under a different state.

That distinction changes how I think about scale.

The valuable unit isn't simply another trajectory. It is another useful part of the task distribution covered by that trajectory.

This also explains why task generation and distributed collection complement each other. A large contributor network can increase throughput, but TaskGen determines where that throughput is directed. Randomization creates the variation; contributors turn those variations into demonstrations; validation and processing decide which demonstrations become usable training data.

Without the first layer, scaling collection risks producing more of what the dataset already knows.

With it, data production can be aimed at expanding what the dataset actually covers.

content:
what are we actually contributing when we complete an @axisrobotics trajectory?

I think this is important to understand. and the answer isn’t simply “robotics data.”

let’s look at the post-training results Axis shared today.

out of 660 human interventions, only 161 (24.4%) were verified as useful enough to make it into the training data.

even more interesting:

training on the full human intervention trajectories actually dropped the success rate from 40.0% to 36.7%.

but when training only on the short, verified corrections that actually recovered the robot from a failure state, average success went up to 48.3%.

so the real takeaway for me is pretty simple:

collecting robotics data ≠ collecting useful robotics data.

even a trajectory that eventually succeeds can contain pauses, unnecessary movements, early interventions, or actions the robot never really needed to learn.

just because we manage to finish the task doesn’t mean the entire trajectory is worth teaching to the model.

what Axis is doing here is more interesting.

the robot runs on its own policy ➛ it starts failing ➛ a human steps in ➛ the correction is replayed and verified ➛ only the parts that actually put the robot back on track become training data.

so when we complete these trajectories, our real contribution isn’t just showing a robot how to do a task from start to finish.

it’s showing the robot where its own policy fails and how to recover from that failure.

and imo that’s the important part of these results.

more data ≠ better data.

sometimes a few seconds of the right correction can be more valuable than an entire successful trajectory.

if you want to see what an Axis trajectory actually feels like, you can try it here: https://t.co/GvODyJjo9A

content:
For weeks I wanted to write about Axis, but every time I started, I felt like I was overcomplicating it.

Today, I'll try my best to explain why I think @axisrobotics is worth paying attention to.

The first thing that caught my attention wasn't the number of robots, trajectories or simulations.

It was the idea of learning from failure.

A robot can perform the same task hundreds of times and still fail when something changes.

> A different object.
> A different position.
> A different environment.

Instead of treating that failure as useless, Axis is building a loop around it.

Robot fails > human corrects it > correction becomes training data > model improves.

Then the improved model encounters new failures, creating another round of useful data.

In my opinion, this is one of the more interesting problems to solve in Physical AI.

Because eventually, the challenge won't just be collecting more data.

It will be figuring out which data the robot actually needs next.

And that's the part of Axis I'm going to be watching closely.

There's also an ongoing @KaitoAI campaign if you want to explore Axis and contribute to the conversation:

content:
ActionFi is an interesting shift in how AI training can work.

Instead of simply giving away your clicks, browsing behavior and actions for free, @ActionModelAI lets users complete real tasks on real platforms, have those actions verified by AI, and earn points toward $LAM.

Here’s the part I find particularly interesting 👇

ActionFi uses bounty multipliers based on the commercial value of a platform.

So a task on a high-value enterprise platform can earn significantly more than the same type of activity on a consumer platform.

For example, the docs show multipliers reaching 73x on selected partner platforms, while enterprise tools can carry much higher multipliers than ordinary consumer platforms.

And the rewards can stack.

Your points are calculated using:

Base Task Reward × Platform Multiplier × Epoch Bonus × Tier Bonus × Quality Bonus

That means your strategy matters.

You can:
• Prioritize higher-multiplier platforms
• Build your contribution tier
• Maintain consistent activity
• Complete tasks carefully for quality bonuses
• Take advantage of early-epoch rewards

The process is straightforward:

Install the browser extension → choose an ActionFi task → complete the task → let the AI verify your actions → earn points.

The bigger idea is even more interesting.

The actions people perform today can help train the Large Action Model, while $LAM is designed to represent participation in that ecosystem and provide utility for Actionist AI agents.

So ActionFi isn’t simply “complete tasks and earn points.”

It is an attempt to create a system where human actions become valuable training data, contributors get rewarded, and the resulting AI ecosystem can have community ownership.

If you’re interested in the intersection of AI agents, human-generated training data and crypto incentives, ActionFi is worth studying.

content:
Axis robotics V2 is taking a smarter approach to building better robotics data.

Instead of endlessly collecting more examples, the system first lets the policy attempt a task independently. 

When it hits a failure point, a human contributor steps in and provides the correct action.

That intervention doesn’t go to waste. It becomes fresh training data that helps strengthen the policy.

As the model improves, its remaining weaknesses become easier to identify. Those weak spots then guide the next wave of data collection and training.

So the loop becomes:

Model attempts → weaknesses emerge → humans correct → new data is created → model improves → new weaknesses are discovered.

That’s the part I find most compelling about Axis V2.

The data pipeline evolves alongside the model, continuously targeting the areas where improvement matters most.

Smarter models don’t just need more data. They need the right data at the right time.

title:
Three AI models give you the same answer. Feels safe, right? Like getting a second and third opinion that all line up.

Here's the part worth slowing down on: agreement between models is not the same
content:
Three AI models give you the same answer. Feels safe, right? Like getting a second and third opinion that all line up.

Here's the part worth slowing down on: agreement between models is not the same as correctness.

Different AI models often share training data. They read the same internet, the same popular explanations, the same repeated claims. So when three models agree, sometimes they're reasoning independently and landing in the same place. Other times they're all pulling from the same source, including the same gap or the same widely repeated mistake.

Agreement built on a shared blind spot still looks like agreement. It just isn't extra evidence. It's one flawed assumption wearing three faces.

This matters most when the question sits on top of assumptions you can't see. A confident, unanimous answer about a niche topic, an edge case, or something that changed recently can feel rock solid and still be built on outdated or incomplete info that every model happened to absorb.

So how do you use consensus without overtrusting it?

Look at why the models agree, not just that they agree. If they reach the same answer through different reasoning, that's stronger. If they all rest on one shared claim, that claim is the thing to check.

Watch for what's missing. Sometimes every model skips the same caveat or ignores the same tradeoff. The silence is the signal.

This is where seeing the full picture helps. @TruthAgentAI compares multiple models on one question and shows the reasoning behind the consensus, not only the final answer. It surfaces where the models actually align, where the agreement is thin, and how much confidence the answer really deserves.

Consensus isn't useless. It's useful evidence when you can see what's underneath it. The goal isn't to distrust agreement, it's to know whether three models agreed because the answer is solid or because they all read the same page.

Next time three models line up, treat it as a strong hint, then check the reasoning before you act on it.

Curious how often consensus holds up once you can see the reasoning behind it: https://t.co/sLLiRTMkwh

Robots don’t learn the way language models do.

Text is everywhere. Physical experience isn’t.

A robot has to figure out how objects behave, how actions change the world, how to recover when things go wrong, and how the same task looks in different conditions. That kind of data is expensive and scarce when it only comes from hardware bound teleoperation.

@axisrobotics is trying a different route.

Instead of limiting training data to people with robots, they open the process through a browser. Users generate trajectories in simulation.

 Those trajectories get processed and augmented. The resulting data feeds robotics models.

The interesting part isn’t just making data collection easier.

It’s building a compounding engine for Physical AI.

Better data produces better models.  
Better models surface clearer data needs.  
The loop keeps feeding itself.

The next leap in robotics may not come from a more advanced machine.  
It may come from a much larger, continuously improving data engine.

What @ActionModelAI  Actually Measures

The interesting part of ActionFi isn’t the reward pool.

It’s the **verification layer underneath it.**

Most Web3 incentive systems optimize for attention, impressions, posts, or wallet clicks. 
#ActionFi is trying to price something harder to fake: **verified execution.**

A partner defines a browser-native workflow. The user enters through the Action Model extension, performs the task, and the extension observes the UI/DOM state, interaction sequence, inputs, and completion conditions.

No API dependency. No custom SDK requirement.

That means the task can be almost anything a human can execute through a web interface: liquidity deployment, protocol configuration, trading flows, onboarding, contract interaction.

Once the workflow reaches its verification state, **$LAM points are credited.**

Here’s the deeper loop:

**Real action → verified trajectory → training data → better Action Model → stronger agents → more useful actions.**

That is why #ActionFi is more interesting to me than another quest layer.

The incentive is attached to **execution traces**, not vanity metrics.

And getting started is simple:

Sign up → install the extension → open ActionFi → choose a task → Start Training → complete the workflow → get verified.

25 August is where this gets interesting.

Because if the reward layer scales with real execution, #Web3 incentives may finally start measuring work instead of noise.

content:
I went through @Chronara_ai latest Build Week update, I realised the interesting part isn’t any single product. It’s how the pieces are starting to connect.

Take Hyvia.

You give it a UK address and it produces a planning appraisal in minutes, but the interesting work is happening underneath.

Hyvia now attaches sources to verified facts, cross-checks government records and the EPC register, and explains discrepancies instead of simply presenting a number. It even found 578 heritage entries in Southwark’s local list that weren’t present in national datasets.

Then there’s the AI layer.

Chronara now has three local models running on its own hardware, but they’re not being called production-ready just because they can generate answers.

They first shadow external models. Their outputs are tested against fixed standards, and they only earn real workloads after meeting those standards. If performance slips, they can be demoted.

The goal is around 90% local, while external models remain the teacher and benchmark, this is where Hyvia connects back in.Human-reviewed and corrected reports are now feeding into the local-model training loop.

So you have real work → expert review → training data → better local models.

Underneath that sits the Supernode network: Chronara’s private mesh connecting sites in London and Manila, with both nodes live and carrying real traffic.That’s what makes the sovereignty story more tangible.

But Chronara is also clear about what isn’t finished. The local models still need manual restarts, monitoring has been unstable, backups need attention, and failover hasn’t yet been proven.

So I wouldn’t call this a finished sovereign AI stack. I’d call it a controlled system being built layer by layer application, data, models and infrastructure , with each layer having to prove itself before production.

That’s what stood out to me from this Build Week.

content:
お、組織でやったわけではなかったということっぽいですね

Nvidiaサーバー密輸事件！Supermicroによる独自調査結果が発表されました。

今年3月、スーパーマイクロの幹部がNVIDIAのAIチップを中国に密輸したとして告発された。スーパーマイクロは、同社の取締役会の独立取締役による内部調査が完了したと発表した。この調査は、当時同社と関係があった3人に対して3月に提起された訴訟に関連するものだった。3月19日、同社は従業員2人と契約社員1人が米国の輸出管理規則に違反する共謀の疑いで起訴されたことを知った。スーパーマイクロは訴訟の被告には含まれておらず、違法行為で告発されたわけでもない。同社は迅速に対応し、3人はもはやスーパーマイクロと関係がない。

スーパーマイクロ社は、今回の調査は同社の筆頭独立取締役であるスコット・エンジェル氏と取締役会監査委員会の委員長であるタリー・リウ氏が主導し、法律事務所マンガー・トールズ＆オルソンLLPが実施したと発表した。同社はフォレンジック会計コンサルタントとしてアリックスパートナーズLLPを起用し、両社は今回の調査において「独立アドバイザー」として活動した。調査結果は独立取締役および取締役会全体に提供済みである。

Supermicro社は、連邦大陪審の起訴状に記載された顧客取引、および規制対象製品を購入した他の顧客との取引を調査した結果、起訴状に記載された不正流用、または規制対象製品の不正流用を認識していた現職の上級管理職はいないことが判明したと発表した。また、同社が輸出規制対象製品を既知の制限対象企業または地域に直接販売した証拠も見つからなかった。

さらに、調査の結果、規制対象製品の移転の可能性が、同社が過去に公表した財務報告書の信頼性に影響を与えるという証拠は見つかりませんでした。調査期間中、規制対象製品の売上増加に伴い、Supermicroは輸出コンプライアンス体制を構築し、運用を開始しました。同社のコンプライアンスチームは、誠実さと倫理的行動の原則を遵守し、経営陣の支援を受けながら、輸出管理対象製品が規制対象企業または地域に移転されるリスクを最小限に抑えることに尽力しています。

今回の調査において、Supermicroは、営業、技術サポート、事業開発部門の従業員に対し、会社の方針や行動規範に違反したとして雇用契約を解除するなど、複数の人事措置を講じた。

Supermicroは、独立アドバイザーの支援を受け、独立取締役が同社の輸出コンプライアンス体制強化のための提言を行い、取締役会がこれらの提言を全面的に採用したと発表した。Supermicroは、法務顧問兼最高コンプライアンス責任者の監督の下、内部レビューを実施し、提言の一部を既に実施済みである。残りの提言の実施については、独立取締役が監督する。

スーパーマイクロの筆頭独立取締役であるスコット・エンジェル氏は、独立調査が完了したことを明らかにした。独立取締役らは、社内の方針や手続きの強化、および今後の様々な改善策を支援するために会社が講じた措置を支持している。

Supermicroは、最高水準のコンプライアンス基準を遵守し、業界全体における製品移行の課題への対応と解決に尽力します。さらに、当社は関係政府機関による調査への協力と支援を継続します。

content:
「最終判断は人間が行う」というヒューマン・イン・ザ・ループ（HITL）は、AIの利用指針などでよく見る原則です。責任の所在をはっきりさせる設計として広く採用されています。

拙著『AGI』では、この原則がむしろ責任の偽装に転じうる危うさを論じました。

人間が実質的に判断できない状況で、最終判断権だけを形式的に持たされると、「人間が決めた」という形式は免罪符として働きはじめます。

しかもこれは、運用の工夫で直る問題ではありません。人間の認知帯域は生物学的に有限です。AIとの速度差は、素子の切替速度で6桁。価値観の書き換えのような遅い過程まで含めればそれ以上の時間スケールの差があります。システム全体を人間の速度に律速させる設計は、AIが強力になるほど許容が難しくなるでしょう。

では、どうするか。本書では、人間をループの中ではなく、上に置くヒューマン・オーバー・ザ・ループ（HOL）二層モデルを提案しています。実行と日常的な判断はAIが担う「速度層」に任せ、人間は遅さがむしろ機能となる「正統性層」に立って、価値の設定、目的関数の更新、そして拒否権を握る。責任は消すのではなく、正統性層に集めて再配分する、という設計です。

実はこの本自体が、HOLの実験的な実装として作られています。草稿の生成や事実確認の補助といった速度層はAIが担い、何のために何を書くか、どの論証を採るか、そして最終責任を誰が負うかという正統性層は、著者の私が担いました。制作方法の詳細は特設サイトで開示しています。

HOLは単体の道具ではありません。本書の後半で論じた構成的多元主義という、より大きな制度原理の実装の一つです。単一の主体にも、単一の尺度にも、世界を委ねないというこの原理については、また改めて書きます。

content:
【8月21日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・ChatGPT Images 2.0 APIが透過画像生成に対応
・高性能ステルスモデルOx Alphaが無料公開
・ロボット基盤モデル「GEN-1.5」がOne-Shot学習を実現
・ClaudeのComputer UseやSkills APIがGAに
・Grok Buildが全有料ユーザーに公開
・Nvidia、韓国Rebellionsと協業協議か
・Azure OpenAI Design Patterns v3.5.0がリリース
・米国でデータセンター建設への反対運動が激化
・Anthropicデータ保持ポリシーの詳細判明

===

ChatGPT Images 2.0 APIが透過画像生成に対応

・OpenAIがChatGPT Images 2.0のAPIで透明な背景（透過画像）を持つ画像を生成できる機能をプレビュー公開しました
・生成された画像は、ウェブサイト、スライド、ゲーム、プロダクトモックアップなどに直接利用可能です
・開発者からは、ステッカー作成やデザイン作業が非常に捗ると歓迎の声が上がっています

===

高性能ステルスモデルOx Alphaが無料公開

・1Mトークンのコンテキストウィンドウやマルチモーダル入力をサポートするステルスモデル「Ox Alpha」が無料公開されました
・DeepSWEベンチマークでFable 5やGPT-5.6 Solを上回るスコアを記録したと報告されています
・コミュニティでは、Zhipu AIの次世代モデル（GLM-5.4や5.5など）ではないかと推測されています

===

ロボット基盤モデル「GEN-1.5」がOne-Shot学習を実現

・物理データで大規模に事前学習されたロボット基盤モデル「GEN-1.5」が発表されました。
・数秒で新しいタスクを学習し、一度のデモンストレーション（One-Shot）で汎化する能力を持っています。
・8ヶ月以上継続して学習されており、シミュレーターの動画でもFew-Shotの例として機能することが注目されています。

===

ClaudeのComputer UseやSkills APIがGAに【続報】

・AnthropicのClaude Platformにおける「Computer Use」などの続報です
・Computer Use、Skills API、Files APIが一般提供（GA）となりました
・1ターンでクリックやタイピングなどの複数アクションを実行可能になりました
・タスクあたりの往復回数が20〜40%削減され、処理の高速化とAPI利用コストの低減が期待されています

===

Grok Buildが全有料ユーザーに公開【続報】

・xAIの「Grok Build」に関する続報です
・SuperGrokおよびX Premiumの全ユーザー向けに公式に提供開始されました
・Web版ではAPIキーを作成せずにSpaceXAIのAPIを直接呼び出すことが可能です
・今後、クラウドエージェント向けのタスクスケジュール機能も追加される予定です

===

Nvidia、韓国Rebellionsと協業協議か

・Nvidiaが韓国のAIチップ設計企業Rebellionsと、技術提携や投資、買収を含む初期段階の協議を行っていると報じられました
・また、米国の輸出規制に対応した中国向け新AIチップについて、年内に小ロット出荷を計画しているとの続報もあります
・AIハードウェア市場におけるNvidiaの戦略的な動きとして注目を集めています

===

Azure OpenAI Design Patterns v3.5.0がリリース

・Azure OpenAIのアーキテクチャ設計パターン「v3.5.0」がリリースされました。
・API Management（APIM）をAI Gatewayとして利用したマルチリージョンフェイルオーバーや、優先度付きルーティングなどが実装されています。
・トークンやコストの可視化など、エンタープライズ向けの実践的なアップデートとして開発者から評価されています。

===

米国でデータセンター建設への反対運動が激化【続報】

・米国におけるデータセンター建設反対運動に関する続報です
・一般市民の反対意見が1年で1.8倍に増加し、政治問題化しています
・電力消費や環境への影響が懸念されており、一部の政治家は新規データセンターの建設モラトリアム（一時停止）を支持し始めています
・ハイパースケーラー企業にとって、今後のAI開発やインフラ拡張の大きなボトルネックになる可能性があると指摘されています

===

Anthropicデータ保持ポリシーの詳細判明【続報】

・Anthropicのデータ保持ポリシー変更に関する続報です
・Mythosクラスのモデルにおける30日間のデータ保持ルール自体は維持されることが判明しました
・エンタープライズ顧客が自社インフラでデータを保持・管理できる機能は、Fable safeguardsとして約100社と共同開発中で、今秋に広く展開される予定です

content:
正式に法務省から、AI等を活用したリーガルテックと弁護士法72条との関係について、新たな指針が出されました。

この指針は、単なる「新規ビジネス×規制」について出された指針ではなく、サービスのユーザー自身が、法を解釈する専門家を含むという特殊性。

弁護士や企業法務による「どこまで許されるのか」という解釈が、導入判断だけでなく、プロダクト設計や市場形成にも直接影響していく構造にある。今回、「訴訟等への利用に特化したサービスは認められにくい」という線が示されたことも、現行法についての一つの解釈による結論。

新しいテクノロジーを、既存の法律の射程にどこまで入れ、どこから許容するのか。その解釈次第で、生まれるサービスも市場も大きく変わる。

法律そのものだけでなく、「法律をどう解釈するか」が新しい市場をつくる。リーガルテックは、そのことが最も分かりやすく現れる領域の一つだと思う。
